justification: All substantive articles concern GCK (glucokinase) in glucose metabolism disorders—MODY, neonatal diabetes, and congenital hyperinsulinism—with no mention of bipolar disorder or neuropsychiatric phenotypes. The only article referencing bipolar disorder (PMID 34350475) uses "GCK" as an acronym for "germinal center kinase" family in describing TNIK, which is a homonym and must be dismissed per instructions. There are therefore no human genetic, expression, functional, or animal-model data linking glucokinase to bipolar disorder in this corpus. The co-mention is purely incidental and provides no logical biological basis, supporting a Novel classification.

The only article directly linking GCK (glucokinase) to Alzheimer's disease is a mouse study showing time-restricted feeding improves cognition via a GCK/NPY/apoptosis pathway (PMID 41748034), which is animal/mechanistic evidence rather than human genetic data, supporting "Hypothesized." Several other hits are homonym artifacts: the MINK1 review refers to the germinal center kinase (GCK) family, not the glucokinase gene (PMID 39727954), and "Ginsenoside C-K" is unrelated to GCK (PMID 40510292). The remaining papers concern glucokinase biology in diabetes, hypoglycemia, and insulin secretion (PMIDs 30641049, 30623114, 36384957, 8589523, 24371439) with no Alzheimer's phenotype; diabetes is a risk factor for dementia, but no human study here reports GCK variants associated with AD. No articles report AD patients or families carrying GCK variants, so Established is excluded and Existing is minimally supported.

One human case-control study directly tested the IRS2 1057G/A (Gly1057Asp) polymorphism for association with refractory temporal lobe epilepsy in Han Chinese (PMID 25458098), providing limited but credible human genetic evidence, which fits "Existing" rather than "Established" since there is no independent replication or family-based causal demonstration. The ganglioglioma study (PMID 34355449) reports somatic IRS2 copy-number gain in long-term epilepsy-associated tumors in humans, but this is a somatic CNV in a tumor context and cannot isolate IRS2 causality for epilepsy. Supporting biological plausibility comes from animal work showing altered IRS1/IRS2-dependent PI3K/Akt insulin signaling in the brains of genetic absence epilepsy rats (PMID 32304254) and hippocampus-related behavioral/metabolic changes in Irs2-null mice (PMID 33940386), which would otherwise only support "Hypothesized." Remaining papers concern metabolic, oncologic, or longevity roles of IRS2 and are not epilepsy-relevant. Therefore the weight sits mainly on "Existing," with a substantial residual on "Hypothesized."

No article reports IGF1R variants causing Alzheimer's disease in independent probands or families, so Established is excluded. However, several human genetic studies provide suggestive association evidence: an IGF1R RFLP polymorphism study in dementia cohorts (PMID 16983186, though the significant signal was in vascular dementia females, with only a trend overall), a pathway-based exon-sequencing study in which IGF1R variants modified cognitive impairment/MCI and brain network topology (PMID 28050343), and a large gene–gene interaction analysis of longevity pathway variants in ~20,000 subjects where IGF1R emerged among interacting loci affecting late-onset AD risk (PMID 37621137). Much of the remaining literature is mechanistic/biological—brain insulin/IGF-1 resistance in AD brains (PMID 22476197), IGF1R signaling in AD models (PMIDs 38565402, 26804996, 36776414), and drug-repurposing network analyses (PMID 36604493)—supporting a strong but non-variant-based pathway link. This combination of limited, non-definitive human genetic association plus abundant biological plausibility favors Existing, with substantial residual weight on Hypothesized.

No article reports HNF1A variants in Alzheimer's disease patients, families, or case-control genetic association studies, so Established is excluded. The strongest link is biological/expression-based: HNF1α upregulation driving SLC23A1-mediated ascorbic acid transport in the intestine of 5xFAD transgenic mice (PMID 33672967), which is animal-model data and therefore supports Hypothesized rather than Existing. The peripheral blood biomarker study of shared AD/T2DM/MDD signatures (PMID 36994393) may implicate HNF1A as a transcriptomic hub in humans, but it is expression-based rather than variant-based and only weakly supports Existing. The remaining articles (MODY, congenital hyperinsulinism, lncRNA HASTER/HNF1A-AS1 reviews) concern HNF1A biology in diabetes with no Alzheimer's relevance, though the T2DM link provides an indirect mechanistic rationale. A small residual probability is left for Novel given the incidental nature of several co-mentions.

None of the supplied articles address congenital heart disease. The "CHD" acronym in PMIDs 11286643 and 10389214 refers to coronary heart disease (an acquired atherosclerotic condition), and "CHI/CH" in PMIDs 25733449, 23275527, 23345197, 26316429, 26268944 and 34253504 refers to congenital hyperinsulinism — both are homonym acronyms that must be dismissed. The remaining literature concerns HNF1A in monogenic diabetes (MODY3), hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia, serum urate, and cortisol metabolism, with mouse/islet mechanistic work (PMIDs 27667715, 11065346) unrelated to cardiac development. There is no human genetic or biological evidence linking HNF1A variants to structural congenital heart malformations, so the co-mentions are purely incidental, supporting a Novel classification.

The retrieved literature overwhelmingly concerns HNF1B and the 17q12 deletion/duplication syndrome, where autism features arise from a multigenic copy number change on chromosome 17q12 — a region that does not contain HNF4A (20q13). The only HNF4A-specific papers (PMID 36257325 on MODY penetrance and PMID 25733449 on congenital hyperinsulinism) link HNF4A to diabetes and hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia, with no mention of autism or neurodevelopmental phenotypes. No article reports HNF4A variants in ASD probands or families, so Established and Existing are unsupported. A small weight remains for Hypothesized, since HNF4A is a developmental transcription factor whose paralog/partner network (HNF1A/HNF1B) is implicated in neurodevelopmental syndromes, providing a tenuous biological rationale; otherwise the co-mentions are incidental.

No article reports HNF1A sequence variants in schizophrenia probands or families, so Established is excluded. The only direct schizophrenia link is PMID 33093650, which found elevated peripheral blood expression of the antisense lncRNA HNF1A-AS1 (HASTER) in patients versus controls — human expression evidence at the HNF1A locus, but not variant-based and concerning the antisense transcript rather than HNF1A protein itself, which fits Hypothesized. PMID 38242953 supports biological plausibility by showing HNF1A-AS1/HASTER acts as a cis-regulatory stabilizer of HNF1A transcription, connecting the lncRNA signal to the gene. PMID 26166263 mentions schizophrenia only in the context of PSMD9 variants and MODY3 phenotypes, a homonymous/incidental co-mention providing no HNF1A-schizophrenia variant evidence. All remaining papers concern diabetes, congenital hyperinsulinism, hepatic adenoma, colorectal cancer, or urate levels, which are irrelevant to schizophrenia, leaving residual probability for Novel.

The only article that tests HNF4A against bipolar disorder is the Japanese T2D-GWAS cross-disorder study (PMID 24196380), which found only a nominal, uncorrected signal in the screening stage that failed replication; the authors explicitly concluded no support for shared genetic risk between T2D and psychotic disorders. All other listed papers concern HNF4A in monogenic diabetes (MODY1), congenital hyperinsulinism, gallstone disease, incretin regulation, or ligand discovery, with no link to bipolar disorder. There is a weak conceptual rationale (metabolic comorbidity/T2D overlap with bipolar disorder) that could justify a "hypothesized" relationship, but no positive human genetic evidence and no functional neurobiological data are provided. Therefore the evidence favors Novel, with some weight to Hypothesized and minimal weight to Existing given the failed nominal association.

Multiple independent human studies report HNF1A variants in diabetic probands and families: MODY3 (a monogenic form of NIDDM/type 2 diabetes) mutations segregating in independent UK, German, Danish and other pedigrees (PMID 9075818, 9032114, 9097962, 8945470, 9166684), and penetrance/prevalence work across thousands of probands and population cohorts (PMID 36257325). Beyond monogenic diabetes, large-scale human genetic studies directly implicate HNF1A in polygenic/common T2D: exome-wide significant gene-level association in youth-onset T2D (PMID 38278947), rare ClinVar variant association with fivefold increased T2D risk in 51,256 cases (PMID 39379762), common-variant pleiotropy at rs1183910 (PMID 24442509), and the private G319S variant strongly predisposing to T2D in Oji-Cree adults and adolescents (PMID 12726923, 16276364). Functional β-cell work (PMID 40774250) supports mechanism but is secondary to the human genetic evidence. A minority of weight remains on "Existing" because some of the strongest proband-based evidence concerns MODY rather than classic adult polygenic T2D.

The only article providing a direct mechanistic link is the HDAC2/HNF-4A/miR-101b/AMPK study (PMID 28202389), which shows that HDAC2-mediated deacetylation of HNF-4A disrupts miR-101b promoter binding and drives tau hyperphosphorylation and dendritic/memory deficits — but this is entirely in mouse models and in vitro, with no patient variants. The computational NIM network paper (PMID 29848990) lists HNF4A as a hub for rheumatoid arthritis, not Alzheimer's disease, and is not genetic evidence. The ABCA7 review (PMID 33221536) mentions HNF4α only as a transcriptional regulator of ABCA1/ABCA7 cholesterol handling, an indirect pathway link. All remaining papers concern MODY, renal Fanconi syndrome, hepatic/bile acid regulation, or lipoprotein gene transcription and are irrelevant to AD. Therefore no human genetic association exists, making "Hypothesized" the appropriate category based on biologically relevant functional/animal data.

None of the provided articles address congenital heart disease; the "CHI" acronym appearing throughout refers to congenital hyperinsulinism, not congenital heart disease, and should be dismissed as a homonym. The literature set consistently links HNF4A to monogenic diabetes/MODY1, neonatal/transient hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia, renal Fanconi syndrome, and serum urate regulation, with no cardiac phenotype reported in probands or families. There is no expression, pathway, or animal-model evidence here connecting HNF4A to cardiac development (the only functional work concerns Drosophila nephrocytes and kidney/liver transcriptional regulation). Therefore no causal or associative human genetic evidence exists in this corpus, and only a minimal allowance is left for a hypothesized biological link given HNF4A's broad metabolic/developmental transcription factor role.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report IGF1R coding variation in relation to type 2 diabetes: a large UK Biobank exome analysis found damaging missense variants in IGF1R conferring ~2.4-fold T2D risk with supporting IGF-1 resistance phenotypes and Mendelian randomization (PMID 36530175); a novel G310D variant with functional characterization was associated with T2D in American Indians (PMID 29470850); family-based reports describe heterozygous IGF1R mutations segregating with progressive glucose intolerance and parental T2D (PMID 25153223) and a homozygous IGF1R variant family where heterozygous carriers had short stature and T2D (PMID 26252249). Candidate-gene/cohort studies (PMIDs 15127203, 18249219) also link IGF1R polymorphisms to IGT-to-T2D conversion, though one earlier Danish study was negative (PMID 10770205), and supportive mechanistic/animal data exist (PMIDs 21910970, 28351623). The breadth of independent human probands and families plus a well-powered exome association supports Established, but the modest number of causal family reports and some negative/candidate-gene data leave substantial weight on Existing.

The only human genetic evidence is PMID 41850236, a drug-target genetic association study in two independent Han Chinese schizophrenia cohorts showing that a GCK genetic risk score (proxying glucokinase activation) is associated with lower glucose and poorer symptomatic improvement on PANSS, with replication in a validation sample and proteomic support. This is credible human variant-based evidence linking GCK to a schizophrenia-relevant outcome (antipsychotic treatment response/symptom severity), but it does not demonstrate that GCK variants cause schizophrenia, so "Established" is not supportable (no studies report causal GCK variants in independent schizophrenia probands or families). The remaining papers are either about GCK enzymology/diabetes (PMIDs 30641049, 23271955, 33477627) or concern a metabolic pathway perturbation in a CCL11 animal model of schizophrenia-related cognitive impairment (PMID 40719991), which provides only biological/pathway plausibility. Hence the weight falls mainly on "Existing," with substantial residual probability on "Hypothesized" if the drug-target GRS evidence is judged to concern treatment response rather than disease liability.

No article reports HNF1A sequence variants in bipolar disorder probands or families, so Established is excluded. The only direct link is an expression study showing the HNF1A antisense lncRNA HNF1A-AS1 is under-expressed in blood of bipolar patients with good discriminative AUC (PMID 36463340); this is human expression/biomarker data rather than genetic variant association, which maps to Hypothesized (with some chance a grader counts it as Existing). The PSMD9 papers (PMIDs 22934761, 24648162, 26166263) concern a different 12q24 gene and only mention MODY3 (HNF1A-related diabetes) tangentially, providing no variant evidence for HNF1A in bipolar disorder. The urate GWAS (PMID 31578528) and the lncRNA transcription review (PMID 38242953) establish HNF1A/HASTER biology but are unrelated to bipolar phenotypes. Overall, a plausible but indirect expression-based biological link dominates.

No article reports IGF1R sequence variants or genetic association testing in bipolar disorder patients, so Established is excluded and Existing is poorly supported. The strongest human data (PMID 33274367) is a postmortem subependymal zone expression study in which IGF1 mRNA was reduced in both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, while IGF1R and IGFBP2 reductions reached significance only in schizophrenia — this is expression, not variant, evidence. Supporting biology comes from animal/model work: DISC1 mutant mice show altered pIGF-1Rβ signaling (PMID 32431597) and olanzapine modulates IGF-1/IGF-1R in a rodent bipolar mania model (PMID 41564197), both pointing to plausible pathway involvement without human genetic proof. Other IGF1R papers concern growth disorders, Graves' orbitopathy, cancer, asthma, autism (GIGYF1), and longevity, which are irrelevant to bipolar disorder. Therefore the relationship is best described as Hypothesized.

No article reports variants in HNF4A causing schizophrenia in probands or families, so Established is excluded. The only human genetic study (PMID 24196380) tested T2D GWAS SNPs including HNF4A in Japanese schizophrenia/bipolar samples; the nominal signal (p<0.01) failed replication and the authors concluded no shared genetic risk, which is weak-to-negative evidence rather than a credible positive association. The strongest supportive material is biological: a postmortem human cerebellar proteomic analysis identified HNF4A among 11 enriched transcriptional regulators potentially controlling altered proteins in chronic schizophrenia (PMID 40332239), and a rodent D-serine (NMDA-related) transcriptomic study placed Hnf4a in a network hub of dysregulated genes (PMID 19212759) — pathway/expression-level, not variant-level evidence. Other articles concern monogenic diabetes, urate, cancer proteogenomics, or 17q12 CNVs (which cannot implicate HNF4A specifically) and are incidental co-mentions. This profile best fits Hypothesized, with some residual probability for Existing given the nominal association and Novel given its non-replication.

Nearly all retrieved articles concern GCK in monogenic diabetes (MODY2), permanent neonatal diabetes, and congenital hyperinsulinism, with no link to structural congenital heart disease. The papers mentioning "CHD" (PMIDs 24696842, 32252966) use the acronym for coronary heart disease, a homonymous phenotype unrelated to congenital heart defects, and should be dismissed. The only article co-mentioning congenital heart defects (PMID 20082465) explicitly sequenced GCK among other genes in three patients with pancreatic agenesis and cardiac malformations and found no mutations — negative evidence. Other co-mentions ("congenital hyperinsulinism") are incidental lexical overlaps with "congenital," not cardiac phenotypes. Therefore no human genetic or biological evidence supports a GCK–congenital heart disease relationship.

Only one study (PMID 39376742) reports its own human genetic evidence, finding enrichment of rare IGF1R variants in a Chinese Han ASD cohort and in the SFARI SPARK WES dataset, supported by scRNA-seq and organoid transcriptomics implicating IGF1R in PV interneurons; a single cohort without independent replication supports "Existing" but not "Established." The GIGYF1 papers (PMIDs 35917186, 36189799) show ASD-causal variants in GIGYF1 that disrupt IGF-1R recycling and IGF-1R/ERK signaling — strong mechanistic/pathway support for IGF1R biology in ASD, but the variants are not in IGF1R itself. Pathway reviews (24662006) and Fragile X mouse work (27643697) provide animal/biological plausibility only, and a post-mortem human study (32154665) found no IGF1R expression differences in idiopathic autism, arguing against a pathogenic role. Several other articles (liposarcoma genomics, CRISPR screens, metabolic syndrome, longevity, short stature CNVs) are irrelevant or involve multigene CNVs. Overall the evidence sits between limited human genetic association and strong biological hypothesis.

All human genetic evidence linking IGF1R to congenital heart disease comes from contiguous 15q26 terminal deletions (PMIDs 39816431, 27826649, 34530895, 17931990, 41748325), which span many genes and cannot isolate IGF1R; indeed, one report shows CHD in patients with 15q26.3 deletions that exclude IGF1R and proposes other candidate genes (ALDH1A3, LRRK1, CHSY1, PCSK6; PMID 37434556), arguing against IGF1R causality. Series of patients with intragenic IGF1R point mutations (PMIDs 31586944, 23392101, 27625849) describe growth retardation, microcephaly and IGF-1 resistance, not congenital heart defects, so no two independent probands/families with IGF1R sequence variants causing CHD can be cited. A human amniotic-fluid study implicates reduced amino acids affecting IGF1R signaling in CHD (PMID 30917366), giving a biological/mechanistic rather than variant-based link. Other papers concern cancer, asthma, autism or aging and are irrelevant homonym/pathway co-mentions. The balance therefore favors Hypothesized with substantial weight to Existing based on the recurrent deletion-phenotype co-occurrence.

No article reports HNF1A variants in individuals with autism spectrum disorder. The ASD-related genetic reports here (PMID 36331019, 36700567) concern HNF1B (HNF1-β) within the 17q12 region and multigene CNVs, which are a different gene and cannot implicate HNF1A; these should be dismissed as homonym/neighbouring-gene evidence. The only human ASD measurement involving the HNF1A locus is the lncRNA expression study (PMID 34658787), in which HNF1A-AS1 showed no significant difference between ASD cases and controls — a negative result that provides a tenuous, non-supportive link at best. All remaining HNF1A literature concerns monogenic diabetes (MODY3) and congenital hyperinsulinism, with mechanistic work in mouse and INS-1 cell models, none of which bears on ASD biology. Therefore the relationship is essentially Novel, with a modest allowance for Hypothesized given the measured (though negative) HNF1A-AS1 transcript in an ASD cohort.

No article demonstrates causal IRS2 variants in independent ASD probands or families; the Korean case-control study (PMID 27483248) genotyped IRS2 rs4773092 but found a significant association only for IRS1, so Established is excluded. Human evidence supporting some link includes a suggestive (not genome-wide significant) family-based GWAS signal in the intergenic region between MYO16 and IRS2 in male-only multiplex families (PMID 24132906) and a genome-wide significant placental DNA methylation DMR at IRS2 in a prospective ASD cohort, replicated by pyrosequencing and modified by prenatal vitamin use (PMID 31009952), further summarized in a systematic review (PMID 41120033). These are human data implicating the IRS2 locus epigenetically/positionally rather than through causal coding variants, best fitting "Existing" with substantial residual probability for "Hypothesized" since the methylation finding was genotype-independent and the GWAS hits were intergenic. Remaining articles concern IRS2 in metabolism, insulin resistance, cancer, or rodent hippocampal behavior (PMID 33940386), which support biological plausibility only.

None of the provided articles mention Autism Spectrum Disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype; all concern GCK's role in glucose homeostasis, monogenic diabetes (MODY2, PNDM), congenital hyperinsulinism, gestational diabetes, and enzyme structure/regulation. There are no human genetic studies linking GCK variants to autism, and no probands or families with ASD are described, so Established and Existing are unsupported. A very weak indirect biological rationale could be argued (neonatal hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia causing brain injury, or maternal gestational diabetes as an ASD risk factor), which justifies a small allocation to Hypothesized, but these connections are not made in any of the cited abstracts. The co-mentions here are incidental, making Novel the most appropriate category.

No article in this set reports HNF1A variants identified in epilepsy probands or families; there is therefore no basis for "Established". The only human-variant route to seizures is indirect: HNF1A is listed among the nine genes whose mutations cause congenital hyperinsulinism/hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia (PMIDs 26268944, 23275527, 25733449, 26316429, 34253504), and a review explicitly notes that CHI-related hypoglycaemia produces brain injury and "secondary epilepsy" (PMID 27921429) — a recognized acquired risk factor rather than direct epileptogenesis, and in HNF1A specifically the hyperinsulinism is typically transient/mild with later MODY (PMID 25733449). The 17q12 seizure phenotype (PMID 19844256) involves HNF1B within a multigene deletion and cannot implicate HNF1A. Remaining papers (MODY, pharmacogenetics, lncRNA/HASTER, MTTP promoter) are diabetes-focused and provide no epilepsy link, so probability is split between a weak indirect human association (Existing), a purely biological/mechanistic rationale (Hypothesized), and incidental co-mention (Novel).

Activating GCK variants cause congenital hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia, and recurrent neuroglycopenia is a well-recognized mechanism/risk factor for seizures and epilepsy, which fits the "Existing" definition. The strongest primary human evidence is PMID 34635134, which reports three drug-unresponsive GCK-HI patients with intellectual disability and refractory epilepsy treated with ketogenic diet, supported by PMID 31094068 describing GCK-activating CHI cases. Most other papers (22231386, 23776849, 24931352, 23275527, 39245718) merely list GCK among CHI genes and mention epilepsy as a generic complication of untreated hypoglycaemia — background citation rather than gene-specific evidence. PMID 22043488 involves a ~12 Mb 7p13-15 deletion encompassing GLI3 and GCK, so the epilepsy/mental retardation cannot be attributed to GCK. Because the epilepsy is a secondary consequence of hypoglycaemia and replicated independent GCK-specific epilepsy cohorts are lacking, Established is unlikely.

No article in this set reports HNF4A variants as a direct cause of epilepsy in independent probands or families; the single case in which an HNF4A variant was found in a teenager with seizures (PMID 37664540) was explicitly reassessed and downgraded to "likely benign," which is negative evidence. The main human genetic evidence is that heterozygous HNF4A mutations cause congenital/transient hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia (PMIDs 23275527, 23345197, 33770274, 25733449), a recognized cause of neonatal seizures and of subsequent epilepsy/neurological impairment if untreated — a well-established precursor/mechanism, which fits "Existing." The pharmacogenetic papers (PMIDs 26213157, 27610747, 28837897, 30169477) link HNF4α polymorphisms only to antiepileptic drug concentrations/response in epilepsy patients, not to epilepsy risk, providing indirect, phenotype-adjacent support at best. Since the causal link to epilepsy itself is mediated through hypoglycaemic brain injury rather than demonstrated directly, Established cannot be supported with two qualifying PMIDs, and a substantial share of probability remains on Hypothesized.

One human genetic study reports an IRS2 polymorphism (rs4773092, Cys816Cys) associated with auditory hallucinations in schizophrenia patients (PMID 23706954), which constitutes a single credible but non-replicated human variant-level association with a schizophrenia-related phenotype — supporting "Existing". Additional human evidence is biological rather than genetic: patient-derived olfactory neuronal cells from schizophrenia and bipolar patients show reduced IRS2 tyrosine phosphorylation, with Irs2 knockout mice displaying aberrant amphetamine responses (PMID 33173197), supporting a mechanistic/pathway link. Remaining articles concern insulin resistance, metabolism, cancer, PCOS, or antipsychotic-induced metabolic effects and are not direct genetic evidence for schizophrenia. Because no two independent human studies demonstrate variants causing schizophrenia in separate probands or families, "Established" is not supportable; residual probability is placed on "Hypothesized" given the predominance of mechanistic and animal data.

No study demonstrates a replicated causal link between IGF1R variants and schizophrenia; the only direct human genetic finding is a single clinically significant IGF1R variant reported in one childhood-onset schizophrenia proband in a diagnostic exome series (PMID 36645932), which is suggestive but far from replication, and a dedicated candidate-gene pooling study found no association of the IGF1R functional SNP with schizophrenia (PMID 17044098). Supporting but non-genetic human evidence includes reduced IGF1R mRNA in the subependymal zone of patients (PMID 33274367), increased anti-IGF1R antibody reactivity in CSF/serum of psychosis patients (PMIDs 34506098, 40319454, 37776553), and altered IGF1R expression in PBMC signaling studies (PMID 41843846) and suicide/psychiatric transcriptomic analyses (PMID 37794117). Animal/mechanistic work (ketamine NMDAR-hypofunction mice, Disc1 mutants, GIGYF1–IGF-1R signaling; PMIDs 29137928, 32431597, 35917186) supports biological plausibility only. Several listed papers (liposarcoma genomics, longevity, pediatric cancer, IGF1R growth defects) are irrelevant to schizophrenia. Overall the evidence sits between "Existing" (one human variant report plus human expression/autoimmune findings) and "Hypothesized."

No article reports pathogenic IGF1R point variants in patients with epilepsy; the IGF1R coding mutation literature (PMIDs 31586944, 27625849, 23392101) concerns growth retardation/IGF-1 resistance, not seizures. The only genetic links to epilepsy come from 15q26 terminal deletions and other contiguous-gene rearrangements (PMIDs 27826649, 29226546, 23815819), which span many genes and cannot implicate IGF1R specifically — and one of them explicitly excludes IGF1R from the deleted interval. The strongest evidence is mechanistic: IGF-1/IGF1R signaling promotes epileptiform and seizure activity in rodent models and increased IGF1R activation is seen in human epileptogenic tissue (PMID 26286172), IGF1R modulation alters seizure severity in pilocarpine rats (PMID 33095440), circIgf1r knockdown is neuroprotective after status epilepticus (PMID 33417289), and IGF1R regulates neuronal glucose uptake in seizure models (PMID 33258143). This is expression/pathway/animal-model evidence, which fits "Hypothesized," with a modest allowance for "Existing" based on human epileptogenic tissue findings and the multigene 15q26 deletion phenotypes.

No article in this set reports IRS2 sequence variants or genetic association testing in bipolar disorder patients, so Established is excluded and Existing is weakly supported at best. The strongest evidence is PMID 33173197, which found reduced IRS2 tyrosine phosphorylation upon insulin stimulation in olfactory neuronal cells biopsied from bipolar disorder and schizophrenia patients, plus an aberrant amphetamine response in Irs2 knockout mice — this is functional/expression and animal-model evidence, which fits Hypothesized rather than variant-based association. Other papers address IRS2 in insulin resistance, obesity, PCOS, liver metabolism, Parkinson's disease and cancer (PMIDs 12687350, 22523112, 38155330, 32015092), and are relevant only to general IRS2 biology, not bipolar disorder genetics. Papers on olanzapine-induced hepatic insulin resistance (PMID 30550886) merely mention bipolar disorder as a treatment indication, an incidental co-mention. Overall, the biology (insulin signalling in neurons, patient-derived cells, knockout mouse behaviour) provides a plausible mechanistic link without genetic variant evidence.

None of the provided articles address congenital heart disease; the "CHD" appearing in several abstracts refers to coronary heart disease (e.g., PMID 18506362, 35906673), a homonym acronym that must be dismissed. The IRS2 literature here is overwhelmingly metabolic (insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, beta-cell function, hepatic steatosis, longevity), with no human genetic variant linked to cardiac malformation. The only cardiac-relevant data are murine cardiomyocyte-restricted Irs2 deletion causing susceptibility to stress-induced arrhythmia and pressure-overload dysfunction (PMID 39253856), and embryonic growth/developmental roles of IR/IGF-IR–IRS signaling in mice (PMIDs 10417963, 9761714), which could at most support a weak, indirect biological hypothesis rather than a congenital heart defect link. Therefore no Established or Existing (human variant–based) evidence exists, and most probability falls to Novel with a modest allowance for Hypothesized based on developmental/cardiac mouse biology.

Human genetic evidence directly linking GCK to diabetes phenotypes is substantial: the large TOPMed-imputed T2D meta-analysis of 51,256 cases reported a rare ClinVar GCK variant conferring ~8-fold increased T2D risk (PMID 39379762), and exome analysis of 200,000 UK Biobank participants found a gene-based GCK association with cardiometabolic/glycemic disease, replicated in Geisinger MyCode (PMID 35177841). Additional human data include the GCK -30G>A promoter variant associated with fasting/post-OGTT hyperglycemia and impaired glucose regulation in a population cohort (PMID 16186409), HbA1c association in Greenlandic Inuit (PMID 29483669), and multiple independent proband/family reports of GCK mutations causing GCK-MODY, a recognized monogenic diabetes subtype with high penetrance (PMIDs 30257192, 28555465, 36257325, 25555642). However, most proband/family-based evidence pertains to MODY2 rather than common T2D, and early microsatellite association studies in Caucasian and South Indian cohorts were negative or weak (PMIDs 8261750, 8314445, 8359581), so strictly T2D-focused causal replication in probands/families is less clear-cut. This supports a strong but partly subtype/precursor-based relationship, splitting probability mainly between Established and Existing.

Multiple independent human genetic studies directly implicate HNF4A variants in diabetes risk beyond pure MODY ascertainment: a large rare-variant GWAS of 51,256 T2D cases identified the HNF4A p.Arg114Trp missense variant conferring ~8-fold increased T2D risk (PMID 39379762); an exome burden study of 74,629 individuals found enrichment of pathogenic HNF4A variants among people with common T2D (PMID 33046911); a candidate-gene association study examined low-frequency coding variants (T130I, V255M) in HNF4A for T2D susceptibility (PMID 20878384); and a French family study reported a cosegregating V393I missense mutation with impaired insulin secretion in late-onset NIDDM (PMID 9449683). In addition, HNF4A is the proven MODY1 gene with mutations in independent pedigrees (PMIDs 8945471, 9243109, 9294105, 9313765), and MODY is a recognized monogenic subtype frequently misdiagnosed as T2D, with reduced-penetrance variants (PMIDs 36257325, 30665703) blurring the boundary with common T2D. Evidence is replicated in humans across independent cohorts and families, favoring Established, though some weight remains on Existing because much of the strongest causal evidence pertains to MODY rather than polygenic T2D per se.

The bulk of the evidence linking IRS2 to Alzheimer's disease is mechanistic: mouse knockouts (Irs2-/- behavioral deficits, IRS-2 deficiency impairing LTP, IRS-2 deletion delaying Aβ accumulation in Tg2576 mice) and human postmortem expression/phosphorylation studies showing IGF-1R→IRS-2→PI3K signaling resistance in AD brain, which are functional rather than variant-based (PMIDs 33940386, 21955917, 19487308, 22476197, 30964050). One human genetic association study of IRS gene polymorphisms in Turkish late-onset AD patients (PMID 39954137) directly tests variant–AD association, which, if positive, would support "Existing," though the result is not shown in the abstract and it is a single, unreplicated candidate-gene study. Other variant work on IRS2 (Gly1057Asp) concerns obesity, insulin resistance, PCOS and T2DM—conditions that are recognized risk factors/mechanisms for AD (PMIDs 12687350, 34609116), lending partial support for "Existing" by proxy. No two independent human studies demonstrate causal IRS2 variants in AD probands or families, so "Established" is not supportable; points are split mainly between Existing and Hypothesized.

Supporting biology comes from Shank expression/methylation changes in epileptic rat models and reviews of SHANK1-3 in epilepsy-comorbid NDDs (PMIDs 32564287, 36142719), which are animal/background-level rather than definitive human variant evidence. Thus the balance favors "Existing" (one credible human report plus closely linked NDD phenotypes), with substantial residual weight on "Hypothesized."

The strongest evidence for ST18 (Myt3) in type 2 diabetes comes from functional studies: Myt TF inactivation in mouse pancreatic progenitors causes β-cell dysfunction, loss of proliferation and death, deregulated Myt3 translation causes glucose intolerance in mice, and MYT knockdown kills human EndoC-βH1 and primary human β cells (PMIDs 32359405, 40463090, 41539561, 42247169) — this is predominantly mouse/in vitro mechanistic work, supporting "Hypothesized". No article in this set reports SHANK1 variants identified in Alzheimer's disease patients; all SHANK1 variant studies (deletions, missense, truncating variants) concern autism spectrum disorder, neurodevelopmental disorders, epilepsy, or PKU modifiers, so Established is effectively excluded. Overall the weight of evidence is biologically plausible but not variant-based in AD patients.

Multiple independent human studies report sequence-level SHANK1 variants in ASD probands: a Chinese ASD cohort identified de novo mutations in SHANK1 (PMID 27824329); a targeted sequencing study of 615 ASD patients versus 503 controls found a recurrent, ASD-specific missense variant (p.R874H) with supportive in vitro and knock-in mouse validation (PMID 35388181); truncating SHANK1 variants were characterized in patients with a neurodevelopmental/autistic spectrum phenotype (PMID 34113010); and a de novo mosaic missense variant was reported in a patient with autism and epilepsy (PMID 34912368). A large meta-analysis also detected SHANK1 truncating mutations in ASD males with normal IQ, albeit at very low frequency (~0.04%) and with the caveat that clinical relevance is not fully ascertained (PMID 25188300). The seminal CNV report (PMID 22503632) involves deletions and therefore does not by itself pinpoint SHANK1, and mouse knock-in work (PMIDs 35388181, 37880287) supports mechanism rather than human causality. Given replication across independent probands with point mutations but residual uncertainty about penetrance and rarity, evidence sits between Established and Existing, leaning Established.

No study in the list reports TCF7L1 variants causing Alzheimer's disease in independent probands or families, so Established is excluded. The strongest human genetic evidence is PMID 38135866, which exome-sequenced 82 sporadic AD patients and found common variants in Wnt/TCF-LEF family genes, with TCF3 (TCF7L1) ranking among the top genes affecting cortical thickness—an AD-relevant endophenotype; this is a single, small, non-replicated study, consistent with "Existing" at best. Supporting but non-genetic human evidence comes from PMID 25680440, showing altered Tcf7l1/Tcf3 transcript and protein levels in AD entorhinal cortex and hippocampus, and from mechanistic work linking β-catenin/TCF signaling to Aβ-induced neuronal apoptosis (PMID 17234346), which are pathway/expression arguments typical of "Hypothesized." Other TCF7L1 papers concern pituitary development, ESC self-renewal, colorectal cancer, facial asymmetry, or Parkinson's variants and are not AD-relevant. Points are therefore split mainly between Existing and Hypothesized, with the balance slightly favoring Existing because of the human variant–endophenotype association.

No article reports TCF7L1 sequence variants associated with or causing type 2 diabetes in human probands or cohorts; the human variants described (p.R92P, p.R400Q) relate to congenital hypopituitarism, not diabetes (PMID 26764381). The strongest diabetes-relevant data are biological: TCF3/TCF7L1 and other Wnt components are upregulated in islets of human type II diabetic patients (PMID 19165345), and Tcf7l1 is expressed in rodent pancreas with expression suppressed by insulin and high-fat diet feeding (PMID 20675304), alongside the well-known TCF7L2 paralog link (PMID 29314572). TCF7L1 biology is directly pathway-relevant (Wnt/β-catenin, TCF/LEF repression; PMIDs 22111711, 32989053), supporting a hypothesized rather than established or existing genetic relationship. Remaining papers concern stem cells, cancer, pituitary development, or unrelated acronyms (e.g., E-protein/TCF3 immunology homonyms) and do not provide T2D variant evidence.

No human genetic study links TERF2 variants to autism spectrum disorder in this set; the only ASD-specific article (PMID 40272729) measures Trf2/Trf1 expression and telomere length in the valproic acid rat model after pharmacological treatment, which is animal functional data rather than human variant evidence. Supporting biological plausibility comes from TRF2's role in neuronal differentiation, survival, and DNA damage responses (PMID 17207936) and in shelterin-mediated telomere protection (PMIDs 26871633, 16880378), together with telomere shortening reported in ASD. Human TERF2 variant associations exist only for unrelated phenotypes such as type 2 diabetes (PMID 32296102) and general population-genetic surveys (PMID 16110488), which do not bear on ASD. Therefore the relationship is best described as hypothesized based on mechanism and an animal model, with a small residual chance that reviewers would consider the co-mentions incidental (Novel).

The only article directly linking TERF2 to epilepsy-relevant biology is the mouse study showing that Trf2 downregulation in hippocampal neural cells triggers an excitotoxicity-like phenotype (glutamate overexpression, behavioral alterations) and that Trf2 overexpression protects against post-hypoxic brain damage (PMID 39128227) — this is animal/in vitro functional evidence, not human genetic evidence. A related review highlights TRF2's role in neuronal differentiation/survival and DNA damage responses (PMID 17207936), supporting biological plausibility only. Human genetic association studies of TERF2 variants concern type 2 diabetes, lung cancer, breast cancer survival, aplastic anemia, AMD and dyskeratosis congenita — none involve epilepsy. Therefore no human probands or families establish or even associate TERF2 variants with epilepsy, placing the relationship firmly in the Hypothesized category, with a small residual chance it is considered merely incidental (Novel).

One human candidate-gene case-control study (PMID 32296102) reports a significant association of the TERF2 variant rs4783704 with type 2 diabetes in a Northwest Indian population after Bonferroni correction, and a related prospective study of 11 telomere-pathway loci including TERF2 in the Women's Genome Health Study (PMID 21665207) addressed the same question. A review (PMID 27816684) restates TRF2/TERF2 among telomere maintenance genes implicated in T2D, but this is background citation rather than independent evidence. Thus there is at least one credible human genetic association, but no replication across independent cohorts, so "Established" is not supported. Remaining articles are cancer, neurodegeneration, aging, or in vitro/animal telomere biology studies irrelevant to T2D causality, supporting only a small weight for "Hypothesized."
